meta.title: Residential smart-home energy system reference system
meta.summary: Fictional single-family home in Germany with a PV array, three 10 kWh batteries, a hybrid inverter, a heat pump, a hot-water heating element, a bidirectional 11 kW AC charger, a home energy manager and a flex service. The dashboard shows how a system passport and its component passports serve a homeowner and an installer: user information, registrations, alerts, energy, batteries and services, with the regulatory dashboards under Compliance. All companies, values, statuses and registrations are illustrative; the page states no conformity and no real registration.

nodes.summary: Smart meter (mME) and smart meter gateway (SMGW) at the grid connection of the home. The metering point operator installs, owns and administers them; the homeowner does not. The gateway carries measured values to the entitled parties and control signals to the HEMS. All values are formats or examples; no real identifier is shown.

md.label: Meter system type
md.value: Modern measuring device (mME) plus smart meter gateway (SMGW), together an intelligent measuring system (iMSys), with a control unit where control is required

md.label: Meter number (Zählernummer), format DIN 43863-5
md.note: Placeholder, not a real number. Format: 14 characters. 1 character for the sector, 3 letters for the manufacturer code, 2 hex characters for the production block, 8 digits for the serial number. The text of DIN 43863-5 is paywalled; the format comes from a grid operator information sheet. BSI notes that DIN 43849 will replace the standard.

md.label: Market location ID (MaLo)
md.value: not stated (restricted: identifies a household connection)
md.note: Format: 11 digits. Digit 1 names the issuing body, digits 2 to 10 are a serial number, digit 11 is a check digit. The grid operator assigns it from the BDEW code service. It stays the same when the supplier changes and is the identifier in market communication. Not shown in a public passport.

md.label: Metering location ID (MeLo, Zählpunktbezeichnung)
md.value: not stated (restricted: identifies a household connection)
md.note: The 33-character Zählpunktbezeichnung is the metering location ID. Structure: country code (2 characters), grid operator number (6 digits), postcode (5 digits) and a counter number (20 characters, letters and digits). The grid operator assigns it once and does not change it. The structure comes from the public draft of VDE-AR-N 4400 (2023-09); the final text is paywalled and may differ.

md.label: Gateway ID (SMGW-ID)
md.value: not stated (restricted: identifies a device at a household)
md.note: Format: a device number under DIN 43849 with sector E, 14 characters without spaces, printed on the front of the gateway housing. The certificates of the smart metering PKI are issued to it. It is not the meter number and it is not linked to the metering location ID. No public register of gateway IDs was found.

md.label: Gateway administrator
md.value: The metering point operator (role by law); example: Messstellenbetreiber (example role, fictional)
md.note: The gateway administrator configures and monitors the gateway and sets up which party receives which data. The name of the real party is not shown in a public passport.

md.label: Gateway interfaces
md.value: HAN (local devices, technician and consumer access), LMN (meters), WAN (market participants and gateway administrator)

md.label: Controllable local systems (CLS)
md.value: Machine-to-machine channel through the gateway. Authorised market participants read and control devices over a secure channel that the gateway administrator sets up.

md.label: Control channel to the HEMS
md.value: Digital interface IF_CLS_CTRL over EEBUS (national minimum, VDE FNN 2025); relay contacts remain allowed in a transition. A HEMS on the digital port counts as one controllable device.
md.note: Which route this home uses is an example (demo assumption).

md.label: Control box (Steuerbox)
md.value: FNN control box or gateway with an integrated control interface. One box serves up to four controllable devices; a HEMS on relays counts as two, on the digital port as one.
md.note: No identifier scheme for the control box was found.

md.label: Section 14a participation (example)
md.value: Example: the home takes part with the EV charger, heat pump, heating element and battery charging; the grid-fee module is not stated
md.note: Taking part is a legal duty for devices commissioned after 2023-12-31 above 4.2 kW (BK6-22-300 no. 3.1). The passport carries no grid-fee module.

packs.applicabilityNote: Applies to products with digital elements with a direct or indirect data connection. Bare cells and modules without data connection are outside scope (assessment from the research; the manufacturer decides). Units placed on the market before 2027-12-11 are covered only by Art. 14 until substantially modified (Art. 69). Declaration of conformity, CE marking, conformity route, technical documentation and user information attach to the product placed on the market and are evaluated on passports with the regulatory role; components built into it are covered by the integrator's declaration. Art. 2 has no Battery Regulation, Machinery or RED exclusion (only medical devices, vehicles, aviation, marine equipment and identical spare parts), so those regimes run in parallel. Hybrid inverter, HEMS gateway, EV charger, heat-pump controller and battery BMS have no Annex III or IV entry (default class, module A) unless their core functionality is Annex III item 17 (smart-home security hub), item 12 (router or modem), item 5 (VPN) or Annex IV item 2 (smart-meter gateway); firewalls or operating systems inside a product do not lift its class (IR 2025/2392 recital 4). header.note: Concept demonstration with example data. Parties, values and ratings are illustrative.

about.label: Connected passport viewer
about.intro: This dashboard is a connected passport viewer. It gives one aggregate view over the passports of this home. The home scene, the hierarchy, the knowledge graph, alerts, registrations, services and user information all draw on passport data.

points.title: One source of data
points.text: Today the dashboard and the passports are generated from the same system specification, so they hold the same values. Nothing is typed twice.

points.title: Not yet a live read
points.text: The dashboard does not read the issued passports on the VERA platform while you look at it. It links to each passport once that passport is active. Reading the issued credentials directly, and checking them, is the next step for a connected viewer.

points.title: What you see is labelled
points.text: Every value carries a status (verified, declared, illustrative or unknown). Unknown is never shown as absent. Values of this fictional home are illustrative unless a source is shown.

points.title: What it does not show
points.text: No personal data, no live measurements and no commercial terms. Status counts, alerts and the knowledge graph are calculated from the passport data and add no data of their own.

about.concept: Concept status. The claim, aggregation and scoped-access mechanisms below are a concept of this project. No text read creates a legal route to claim a product passport into an account or a wallet, and the EU Digital Identity Wallet framework has no product-ownership attestation type yet. What is established law or a published specification is marked with its source; everything else is a proposal.

journey.title: The owner journey
journey.note: From commissioning to a connected dashboard, in six steps. The homeowner acts alone or with the installer.

steps.title: Commission and issue
steps.text: The installer commissions the system. The passports of the components and of the system are issued, and each component carries a data carrier such as a QR code that leads to its passport.

steps.title: Claim the passports
steps.text: The homeowner scans the code of the system passport, alone or with the installer. The installer confirms that these passports belong to this home. There is no standard for this attestation yet.

steps.title: Connect an account or wallet
steps.text: The claim is stored in a user account or a wallet as an attestation that the holder operates these passports. A private owner uses the EU Digital Identity Wallet. A company or public body uses a wallet for legal persons, proposed as the European Business Wallet, with a mandate for the person who acts for it.

steps.title: Verify and aggregate
steps.text: As soon as the claim exists, the viewer checks each passport and builds the home model: scene, hierarchy, alerts, registrations and knowledge graph.

steps.title: Grant scoped access
steps.text: The owner grants each party a scope per data category and period: installer, grid operator, supplier, flex provider, registers, manufacturers. A grant can be withdrawn.

steps.title: Use and stay in scope
steps.text: Each party sees its own view. Duties set by law, such as grid operation, metering and registers, continue by law. Other access ends with the grant.

steps: The claim names the passports of this home by their identifiers.
The viewer reads each passport in the tier the requesting party may see. The public tier is open; other tiers need a grant.
It checks the issuer signature, the status and the version. A value that cannot be checked is shown as such.
It merges the passports into one home model with hierarchy, flows, registers and certificates. Each value keeps its passport and its status.
It applies the consent and access policy. No data outside the scope reaches a view.
Live measured data and control stay at home in the energy manager and the meter gateway. Passports carry static data and snapshots; a live feed needs its own authorised connection.

access.legend: Scoped means limited by a grant, by the law or by the consent named in the cell. Duties set by law continue when consent is withdrawn: withdrawing consent ends only flows that rest on consent or contract (GDPR Art. 7(3)).

lockout.title: How a single provider is kept out
lockout.note: Eight layers, so that no single component provider can send control signals or read private data by itself. The layers are a concept; the sources show what each one rests on.

layers.title: Three planes, three rights
layers.text: Passport data, measured data and control signals are separate. A right on one plane gives no right on another.

layers.title: The energy manager is the gate for control
layers.text: Local control passes through the home energy manager, which keeps the list of allowed senders and their limits. Grid operator control comes through the meter gateway and its control box under the smart metering PKI. A manufacturer cloud has no route into either path.
layers.basis: VDE FNN note 2025 on the control interface; BSI smart metering PKI.

layers.title: Trust by pairing, not by cloud
layers.text: Local devices trust each other by mutual pairing, for example with EEBUS. A vendor cloud account does not create trust with the device of another vendor.

layers.title: Grants instead of standing access
layers.text: Each party reads through a grant with a data category, a purpose and a period. It ends or is withdrawn. Access levels fixed by law, such as the battery passport tiers, can only be narrowed, never widened.
layers.basis: Battery Regulation Art. 77 and Annex XIII; ESPR Art. 9 and 10 set access by role.

layers.title: Data minimisation and sovereignty
layers.text: Household data stays at home. The viewer keeps no copy of private data by default. The owner can access, share and move the data.
layers.basis: GDPR Art. 5(1)(c), 7(3) and 20; Data Act Art. 4 and 5.

layers.title: Signed security updates only
layers.text: A manufacturer may ship signed security updates. The user keeps the opt-out. An update carries no new control right.
layers.basis: Cyber Resilience Act Annex I Part I; the last sentence is concept.

layers.title: Evidence for the owner
layers.text: Every control action is logged at the energy manager, as the grid operator rules already require for reductions, and the owner can see it in the viewer.
layers.basis: BK6-22-300: the record is kept for two years. Showing it in the viewer is concept.

layers.title: Why the cloud is kept off the control path
layers.text: Advisories describe hard-coded credentials and cloud interface flaws in inverter software, and the BSI names manufacturer manipulation of inverters as a risk.
layers.basis: CISA advisory ICSA-25-072-12 on one vendor; BSI position paper on energy sector cybersecurity.

outlook.title: Outlook: building and appliance passports
outlook.note: This viewer is the foundation for a building passport and an appliance passport. The mechanisms stay the same: claim, verify, aggregate and grant scoped access. Building passport and appliance passport are not EU legal terms; they are this project's outlook.

items.title: Building passport
items.text: The home passport becomes the entry of a building passport. The Energy Performance of Buildings Directive defines a digital building logbook (Art. 2(41)) and gives owners direct access to data of the building systems and consent-based sharing with third parties (Art. 16(1)). The transposition date was 29 May 2026, and this project has not checked the German transposition.

items.title: Appliance passports
items.text: Each component passport is an appliance passport in the same structure. Under the Ecodesign Regulation no delegated act sets passport rules for heat pumps, water heaters, inverters or home energy managers. EV chargers appear in the working plan for 2028, and that plan is not law. Energy label data in the product database stays at model level.
items.basis: Regulation (EU) 2024/1781; working plan COM(2025) 187; Regulation (EU) 2017/1369, Art. 12.

items.title: Same mechanisms
items.text: The claim, the wallet attestation, the aggregation and the grants do not depend on the product type. A new passport type adds data and roles, not a new access model.

items.title: Agents on the passports
items.text: Software agents attached to the home passports and to the flex service passport could find, compare, negotiate and contract flexibility for the owner, and understand each other through shared semantics. This is a hypothesis and is set out in the next section with what is established and what is not.

graph.title: What a knowledge graph is
graph.note: A plain explanation, then how the graph is built from the passports, why it needs semantic models and what makes it verifiable.

explain.title: What a knowledge graph is
explain.text: A knowledge graph stores facts as short statements: subject, relation, object. The inverter is part of the home. The home is registered in a register. Every thing has an identifier, so statements from different sources join into one connected picture that people and software can query.

explain.title: How it is built from the passports
explain.text: Each passport names its product by an identifier and lists data points, documents, certificates and links to other passports. The viewer turns each of these into statements and merges the statements about the same identifier. The graph on this page is built this way from the passports and registers in the data. VERA credentials follow the W3C credential data model 2.0, and its templates carry a mapping to an RDF vocabulary. Which proof suite and canonical form it uses has not been checked.
explain.basis: Local VERA API specification and templates.

explain.title: Why semantic models are needed
explain.text: Without a shared model, rated power in one passport and nominal output in another cannot be joined. A semantic model gives each concept an identifier (an IRI), a type and defined relations, so data from different manufacturers merges without guessing and software can check it. RDF is the graph model. JSON-LD writes it as ordinary JSON, with a context that maps field names to identifiers.

explain.title: Models that can be reused
explain.text: SAREF from ETSI, with SAREF4ENER for energy and SAREF4BLDG for buildings. Brick for building metadata. RealEstateCore for real estate. IEC CIM and IEC 61850 for grid and substation data. The W3C Web of Things Thing Description for device interfaces. Catena-X aspect models for industrial passports. None is claimed here as adopted for the EU product passport.
explain.basis: Each model on its own page (ETSI, Brick, RealEstateCore, IEC, W3C, Catena-X).

explain.title: What EU standards say about format
explain.text: Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2026/1736 lists harmonised standards for digital product passports. This project has not read the standards, so whether they require JSON-LD, GS1 or IEC 61406 identifiers is not known.

explain.title: What a verifiable knowledge graph is
explain.text: A graph whose statements each come from a signed W3C Verifiable Credential. The issuer signs the passport data. The viewer checks the signature, that the credential is not revoked and that the issuer is trusted, and only then merges the statements. Each statement stays linked to its credential, so the origin of every fact can be shown. The building blocks are standards. Combining them into one verifiable graph is this project's proposal; no source defines it.
explain.basis: W3C VC Data Model 2.0; Data Integrity 1.0; RDFC-1.0; PROV-O.

standards.what: The graph data model: statements as subject, predicate and object, with IRIs.

standards.what: Writes RDF as JSON. A context maps field names to IRIs.

standards.what: Signed claims by an issuer about a subject: credentials and presentations.

standards.what: Two ways to secure a credential: embedded proofs, or JOSE and COSE envelopes.

standards.what: A canonical form of a graph, so that hashes and signatures are stable.

standards.what: Compact revocation and suspension status of credentials. VERA has its own active and archived status and no status list field was found in its API.

why.title: Tamper-evident data
why.text: A signature over the credential shows whether the data changed after the issuer signed it. A canonical form of the graph keeps hashes stable.
why.basis: Data Integrity 1.0; RDFC-1.0; Regulation (EU) 2024/1781 Art. 11 and Regulation (EU) 2023/1542 Art. 78 ask for integrity of passport data.

why.title: Cyber security
why.text: The viewer accepts only statements it can check, so a forged or altered passport does not enter the graph. The Cyber Resilience Act asks for protection of integrity.

why.title: Compliance evidence
why.text: Each obligation can point to the signed statement that meets it, with issuer, date and status. Auditors and market surveillance read evidence instead of copies.

why.title: Data quality
why.text: Shared models and shape checks catch missing fields, wrong types and impossible values before they reach a dashboard.

why.title: Certificates
why.text: A certificate of conformity becomes a credential of the certification body. Its status shows valid, suspended or withdrawn, and it links to the product it covers. The specimen certificates in this demo carry no number and no signature.
why.basis: Concept. Seals of legal persons are evidence of origin under eIDAS.

why.title: Product safety
why.text: A recall or safety notice could be issued as a credential against a product type or batch and reach every graph that holds it. No source read describes this use.

why.title: Fraud prevention
why.text: A counterfeit certificate, or a passport copied to another product, fails the issuer and status check, and identifiers tie a passport to one product. The effect on counterfeiting has not been measured.

why.title: Limits
why.text: A signature shows who said it and that it is unchanged. It does not show that it is true. Values still carry a status (verified, declared, illustrative or unknown), and trust in an issuer has to be managed.

agents.title: Outlook: agents that negotiate flexibility
agents.note: A concept, not a product. If agents are attached to the home passports, which are semantic knowledge graphs, and to the passport of a flex service provider, they could discover each other, read each other's meaning and agree a service inside limits the owner has set. Benefits are hypotheses: no source tests them.

explain.title: What an agent-to-agent protocol does
explain.text: The Agent2Agent protocol (A2A) was started by Google and given to the Linux Foundation in June 2025. Version 1.0.0 was released in March 2026. It defines an Agent Card that describes an agent, discovery, tasks and messages, authentication schemes and signing of Agent Cards. It defines no domain meaning, no contracts and no payments.

explain.title: Where the meaning comes from
explain.text: The flexibility of a device can be described with existing models. SAREF4ENER v2.1.1 (ETSI TS 103 410-1) models flexibility requests, offers and instructions. The S2 standard and EEBUS cover flexibility on the device side, and OpenADR 3 covers market signals. What is missing is an accepted format for a priced flexibility offer between a household agent and a provider agent.
explain.basis: ETSI SAREF4ENER; S2 standard; OpenADR Alliance.

explain.title: How a negotiation could run
explain.text: The owner agent holds a mandate: which devices, which limits such as the battery reserve and comfort, the price or return it must reach, and when the owner must approve. It discovers provider agents and reads their passports: verified identity, capability and security contact. It matches offers to the capabilities in the home knowledge graph, negotiates inside the mandate, records the agreement with a signed consent, and executes through the energy manager gate.

explain.title: What stays fixed
explain.text: Grid operator reduction under section 14a EnWG takes precedence over market-based control. The lock-out layers apply to agents as to any party: no control right beyond the consent scope, and the energy manager checks every command.

explain.title: The law frames the contract, not the agent
explain.text: Dynamic price contracts and aggregator contracts exist in law: aggregator contracts need text form and full pre-contract information (EnWG section 41e). No text read addresses an AI agent concluding a contract. The AI Act has no explicit high-risk class for a household flexibility agent, and its transparency duty applies where a natural person interacts with the AI system. The Data Act rules on smart contracts cover data-sharing agreements, not flexibility contracts. Who is bound, who is liable and what counts as evidence are open.
explain.basis: Directive (EU) 2019/944 Art. 11; EnWG; Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 Art. 50; Data Act Art. 36.

explain.title: Risks
explain.text: Instructions injected into an agent can hijack it: NIST evaluated such attacks. A2A leaves authorisation to the implementer. Many agents acting alike could create new peaks; only secondary sources describe this. The product liability directive does not compensate pure financial loss. Mitigations in the concept: an owner mandate with hard limits, approval by the owner above a threshold, signed and revocable consent, logging, and the energy manager gate.
explain.basis: NIST CAISI; A2A enterprise features; Directive (EU) 2024/2853.

agents.whyTitle: Claimed benefits and what the evidence shows

why.title: Purchasing power: hypothesis
why.text: An owner agent could compare several offers continuously and move the owner's flexibility to the best one. No source tests agents against simple automation or a fixed tariff, so a gain in purchasing power and a faster payback of the investment are hypotheses. ACER and CEER find that real savings come mainly from behaviour change supported by automation.

why.title: Savings seen in simulations
why.text: A simulation commissioned by a supplier gives 20 to 70 euros a year for a dynamic tariff without an EV or heat pump, 288 euros with an EV, a heat pump and intelligent control, and 985 euros with grid fee incentives. A small battery nets about 50 euros a year, and larger ones do not pay back on tariff arbitrage alone. These are simulations by an interested party, not measured results.
why.basis: Neon for Naturstrom, short study on dynamic tariffs (October 2025).

why.title: Untapped potential for grids
why.text: The potential is large on paper: Agora Energiewende puts flexible household demand in Germany at about 100 TWh by 2035. Realised use is small: 73 percent of EU households were on fixed-price contracts in ACER's 2025 report. The gap between the two is potential, not realised value.

why.title: Barriers
why.text: ACER has published no-regret actions to remove barriers to demand response. Whether shared semantics and agents lower those barriers is a hypothesis.

why.title: Grid stability
why.text: Agents could pool the flexibility of many homes and offer it where the grid needs it. No source shows this working. The network code on demand response is still open, and grid operator reduction under section 14a stays first in priority.
why.basis: Concept; European Commission consultation on the network code on demand response.

why.title: What the passports hold today and what is missing
why.text: They hold flexibility class, capacity, interface, control channel, consent scope, battery reserve level, who can switch off and provenance, as readable statements. Missing for an agent: machine-readable types (identifiers from SAREF or S2), endpoints and pairing identifiers, the agent endpoint and identity, a delegated authority mandate, a signed and revocable consent record, and the provider identifier with its issuer DID. The priced offer itself stays outside the passport.

infra.title: Infrastructure first: the viewer is one view
infra.note: Concept. The passports, the knowledge graph and access control are the infrastructure. The dashboard on this page is one application on top of it. In an agentic home, agents can generate a viewer to the owner's preferences, and they can work with each other under mandates from the owner.

explain.title: The infrastructure
explain.text: Verifiable passports hold what is true about the home, signed by their issuers. The knowledge graph gives that data meaning by shared models and joins it by identifier. Access control decides who may see or do what, for how long, with a record of every action. These three layers are the same for every application.
explain.basis: Concept, built on the standards listed in the knowledge graph section.

explain.title: The viewer is one way to see the system
explain.text: This dashboard is a fixed design that shows the same data to everyone. It is useful for a discussion and for an owner who wants a ready view. It is not the product. Other applications read the same layers, and none of them owns the data.

explain.title: Agents generate the owner's viewer
explain.text: An owner agent can build a viewer to the owner's preferences: the language, the level of detail, what to watch such as cost, comfort, carbon or battery health, when to alert, and how to explain a value. The generated viewer reads only through the access layer, keeps no data of its own and shows every value with its status. It should be a declarative view definition that is checked before it is shown, not code written on the fly.
explain.basis: Concept. A view generated by an agent must not hide the status of a value or the source of a claim.

explain.title: Agents work with each other
explain.text: Authorised agents of the installer, the flex service provider, the asset optimiser and the maintenance provider can talk to the owner agent and to each other through an agent-to-agent protocol. Each agent acts under a mandate from the owner with a scope, limits and a period. The energy manager gate and the audit log apply to all of them.
explain.basis: Concept; see the agent section below for what is established.

explain.title: Why infrastructure matters
explain.text: A new service attaches to the same graph and the same rules without a new integration. A new party needs an identity, a mandate and a way to read the graph. It does not need a new data format, a new portal or a copy of the data.

explain.title: Order of priority
explain.text: Safety and law come first, for example the grid operator reduction under section 14a EnWG. The owner's rules come next. Market optimisation comes last. A mandate never widens a legal limit. When agents conflict, this order decides, and the owner can stop any agent at any time.

explain.title: Delegation of authority
explain.text: The wallet framework lists powers and mandates as an attribute category, which is the closest existing hook for delegating authority. No mandate type for software agents exists yet, and none defines how an agent proves it acts for an owner.

why.title: Telecom services
why.text: The gateway and the energy manager need a reliable connection. A telco agent could watch link health, propose backup connectivity and report outages. It needs the connectivity status, not the energy data.

why.title: Facility management
why.text: Maintenance schedules, warranties, documents and service history are already in the passports. A facility management agent could plan inspections and keep the record for the owner or the property manager.
why.basis: Proposition. The passports carry next service due, warranty and support contact data.

why.title: Insurance
why.text: Certificates, installation quality and maintenance records are evidence for a policy and for a claim. An insurance agent would see selected evidence with the owner's consent, not consumption or occupancy. Whether and how this changes premiums is open.
why.basis: Proposition; no market or legal check made.

why.title: Others
why.text: The same layers could serve a mortgage lender, a municipality, a service technician network or a second-life battery buyer, each with the narrow scope the owner grants.

why.title: Where this stays honest
why.text: These are propositions to test, not products or a checked market. What is established is the standards and law listed in the sections above. Mandates for agents, agent-generated viewers, a common flexibility offer format and the liability among agents are open.

gridOperator.intro: This view shows how a grid operator can reach the home, what it can and cannot do, and what it can read in the passports. It is a reading aid for a talk with a grid operator, not legal advice. Points marked as inference or demo assumption are not established by the sources.

roles.is: Operator of the low-voltage grid the home is connected to.
roles.does: Detects grid problems, triggers a reduction under section 14a EnWG, may remote-control feed-in (EEG section 9) and adjust generation and storage (EnWG section 13a), and checks the connection application.

roles.is: By default the distribution grid operator, or a fallback or third-party operator. The homeowner may choose another one.
roles.does: Installs and operates the meter and the gateway, forwards control commands to the control box, and delivers measured values.

roles.is: A role assigned to the metering point operator (MsbG sections 3, 25).
roles.does: Configures and monitors the gateway, sets up which party receives which data, and deploys certificates.

roles.is: Company that sells PV power or pools flexibility. Not needed for this home.
roles.does: Would act as an external market participant through the CLS channel, with its own role and the household consent. Grid reduction takes precedence over market-based control (BK6-22-300 no. 4.6).

roles.is: The home energy manager of this home (Homeflow Controls, fictional).
roles.does: Receives a total setpoint, distributes it to the devices and keeps a record of applied reductions for at least two years (BK6-22-300 no. 7).

chain.label: Grid state
chain.text: The grid operator finds a current or voltage problem in a network area from real-time values (BK6-22-300 no. 4.1). Standard.

chain.label: Grid operator
chain.text: It triggers the reduction and passes it to the metering point operator without delay, presumed to mean within about five minutes (no. 4.2). Standard.

chain.label: Gateway and control box, through CLS
chain.text: The signal reaches the smart meter gateway of the household and goes on through the CLS channel to the control box or to a gateway with a control interface. Standard: MsbG and BSI TR-03109.

chain.label: HEMS as energy management system
chain.text: The digital interface is IF_CLS_CTRL with EEBUS as the national minimum; relay contacts remain allowed in a transition (VDE FNN 2025). The operator decides per device between direct control and one total setpoint to an energy management system (no. 4.4). That this home is controlled through its HEMS is a demo assumption.

chain.label: Devices
chain.text: The HEMS distributes the total setpoint to the EV charger, heat pump, heating element and battery charging, and keeps the guaranteed minimum. The split is a demo assumption.

chain.label: Feed-in path, in parallel
chain.text: For feed-in, EEG section 9 allows remote reduction in stages. FNN describes relay stages of 0, 30, 60 and 100 % for generation. Whether the inverter is reached through the HEMS or directly is a demo assumption.

canDo.title: Reduce the drawing of controllable devices
canDo.text: Only when a grid problem is documented. Applies to EV charger, heat pump with heating element and battery charging, each above 4.2 kW at low voltage. All participating devices in the network area are treated alike.
canDo.basis: EnWG section 14a; BK6-22-300 Annex 1 nos. 2.4, 4.1 to 4.3

canDo.title: Act within about five minutes
canDo.text: The reduction is triggered without delay; five minutes is the presumed limit.

canDo.title: Control preventively until 2028
canDo.text: Where real-time control is not yet possible: up to 24 months per network area, at most two hours per day, with the minimum power still guaranteed.

canDo.title: Read and reduce feed-in
canDo.text: Read the actual feed-in at any time and reduce it fully, stepwise or stepless once the plant is set up for it. Small plants with a feed-in tariff can have a 60 % cap until the control device is installed and tested.

canDo.title: Adjust generation and storage
canDo.text: Plants from 100 kW, and plants the operator can remote-control, may be adjusted on request with compensation. That a home battery or PV plant below 100 kW falls under this is an inference.

cannotDo.title: Cut a section 14a device to zero
cannotDo.text: The floor is 4.2 kW per device under direct control. Under control through an energy management system a formula applies: 4.2 kW plus (n minus 1) times a simultaneity factor times 4.2 kW.

cannotDo.title: Use section 14a to curtail discharge or feed-in
cannotDo.text: Section 14a covers drawing only. For storage it covers only the charging direction. Feed-in needs the EEG or EnWG section 13a route.

cannotDo.title: Choose devices arbitrarily or bypass the gateway
cannotDo.text: All participating devices in the area are treated alike. Once a smart meter system is installed, control runs through the gateway.

cannotDo.title: Refuse or delay a connection for lack of capacity
cannotDo.text: Missing grid capacity is not a reason. The duty to expand the grid continues.

cannotDo.title: Read household data at will
cannotDo.text: Meter data go only to listed roles for listed purposes. Grid state data (voltage, frequency) only on order of the metering point operator in justified cases. HEMS-internal data such as schedules and comfort settings are part of no duty in the texts read (inference).

duties: Inform about control that takes place, and give text-form notice before preventive control (BK6-22-300 no. 8.2).
Inform the supplier of the household through market communication (no. 8.3).
Publish control per network area each month; first publication from 2025-03-01 (nos. 8.4, 10.7).
Keep the documentation of control for two years (nos. 7.1, 7.3).
Receive advance notice of the commissioning of a section 14a device and of planned power changes from the device operator (no. 8.1; NAV section 19(2)).
Send a timetable for a connection request without delay and the compatibility result within eight weeks after complete information (EEG section 8(5), (6)).
Use the ZEREZ-ID and do not ask for the certificate content another way (NELEV section 4(10)).
Around control: the device operator holds the grid operator free of claims for damage from a compliant reduction; injury and gross negligence are excepted (no. 9).
discussion: Which control route does this operator use for section 14a in its area: direct control per device, or one total setpoint to the HEMS as energy management system?
Does the operator accept EEBUS on IF_CLS_CTRL as the digital route today, and which relay stages apply in the transition?
Which metering point operator serves the home, and when does it plan the smart meter system and the control box (MsbG section 45)? The statute does not give this date.
Are three 10 kWh batteries three controllable devices or one group, and does a group coordinated by the HEMS count as one device? The text groups only heat pump and cooling.
Are three batteries three MaStR units, and does an unregistered battery hold back PV payments? Neither point is settled in the sources read.
Is a remote-controllable PV plant or battery below 100 kW in the scope of the operator in EnWG section 13a, and which resource IDs does the operator assign?
How many market locations and metering locations will the connection have, for feed-in and for draw? The number is unknown until the operator assigns them.
Is discharge of a bidirectional charger into the grid handled as generation under VDE-AR-N 4105, is it a MaStR unit, and what does the operator require?

registers.title: Marktstammdatenregister (MaStR)
registers.why: Every PV unit and every battery is a registration object. Late registration can reduce feed-in payments (EEG 2023 §52, read from the statute page; the amounts were not checked against a current consolidated text).
registers.open: Whether three 10 kWh batteries count as three units or one is open (see the register help on storage expansion).

explain.what: The Marktstammdatenregister (MaStR) is the official register of the Bundesnetzagentur for energy market actors and energy units. Every grid-connected PV unit and every battery unit is entered with its master data. The operator registers once as a market actor (Anlagenbetreiber) and then registers each unit. The result is a registration number per unit.
explain.why: Registration is a duty of the operator (MaStRV §3, §5). Claims to the feed-in tariff fall due only after the units are registered (MaStRV §23(1)). A late entry costs 10 EUR per kW of installed power per month, reduced to 2 EUR per kW once the duty is met (EEG §52). The amounts were read from the statute page and not checked against a current consolidated text.

who.does: Is legally obliged. Owns the market actor entry. Stays responsible for correct data and for the deadline, also when the installer enters the data.
May enter the units on behalf of the operator. Hands the registration confirmation to the operator. Has no duty of its own under the MaStRV.

Checks the fields flagged in the register when the Bundesnetzagentur asks it to, and opens correction requests. Assigns the identification number that the unit data ask for. Some operators ask for the MaStR number before they pay the tariff (single-operator statement).
Has no role in the MaStR. The register does not record manufacturer, type or serial number of PV inverters or batteries. Product identity goes through ZEREZ and the grid connection application.
Runs the register, assigns the numbers, confirms a registration on request and may correct obvious errors. Publishes unit data as MaStRV §15 allows.

steps: Commissioning: the first switch-on at the place of operation starts the one-month clock (EEG §3 no. 30).
Within one month: create a MaStR user account, register as Anlagenbetreiber, then register the PV unit and each battery in the web portal of the Bundesnetzagentur.
Download the registration confirmation from the unit list of the account.
Give the unit numbers to the grid operator. Use the same commissioning date in the MaStR, in the commissioning protocol and in the completion notice.
Answer correction requests of the grid operator, which arrive as tickets.
Report later changes within one month: capacity extension, change of operator, decommissioning (MaStRV §5(3), §7(1)).
explain.consequences: A late entry costs 10 EUR per kW of installed power per month, reduced to 2 EUR per kW once the duty is met (EEG §52). Feed-in tariff claims fall due only after registration (MaStRV §23(1)). A missing, wrong or late entry is also an administrative offence (MaStRV §21). It does not stop the plant from running. Open: whether a missing battery entry also holds back the PV payments (an interpretation, not verified).
explain.suggest: This is a suggestion, not a duty. The passport can pre-fill product and design data: commissioning date, rated power and usable capacity. It can list the fields that only the owner or the installer can supply. It can store the register number and the confirmation date once the owner has them. It can warn when the three batteries show different commissioning dates, because each battery has its own one-month clock. The passport never registers for the owner and never stores a login or a token.

explain.what: The grid operator approves the connection of generation, storage and controllable loads. The installer applies through the web portal of the operator before construction and reports completion afterwards. The forms and data fields follow VDE-AR-N 4105 (Annex F) and the FNN data set. Portal names and status names differ between operators.
explain.why: A generation plant up to 30 kW must be applied for through a standardised web portal since 2025-01-01 (EEG §8); consumption devices since 2024-01-01 (NAV). Work on the customer installation is done by a firm in the installer directory of the operator (NAV §13(2)). Charging equipment must be notified before commissioning (NAV §19(2)).

who.does: Signs the commissioning protocol together with the installer. Reports later changes of power or decommissioning.

Submits the application in two phases, notifies the loads, sends the completion notice and the commissioning protocol, and quotes the ZEREZ-IDs. Must be listed in the installer directory of the grid operator.

Sends a timetable without delay (EEG §8(5)). Within eight weeks after complete information it gives the result of the grid compatibility check, a cost estimate and the information for EEG §9 (§8(6)). Decides on the final approval.
Supplies the unit certificates, the ZEREZ-IDs and the values for the data sheet. Has no direct role in the connection process.
VDE FNN publishes the technical rule and the data set; it does not approve connections. The connection decision stays with the grid operator.

registers.title: ZEREZ unit certificate register
registers.who: Manufacturer uploads; the installer quotes the ZEREZ-ID in the application
registers.why: The register holds the unit and component certificates that the grid operator checks. The household does not enter anything.

explain.what: ZEREZ is the central register of unit certificates and component certificates. The certificates show that a generating unit, a storage unit or a component meets the technical rules for grid connection. FGW e.V. runs the register. A home does not appear in ZEREZ; its products do.
explain.why: Since 2025-02-01 the grid operator must use the ZEREZ-ID and may not ask for the certificate content another way (NELEV §4(9), (10), §7(4)). Without a valid certificate the final approval is refused (NELEV §6(1)), and a running plant can be disconnected after a written notice (§6(2)). The roadmap process V5 is a plan of the Bundesnetzagentur to link the MaStR to ZEREZ; it is not a duty for a home.

who.does: Uploads nothing. Must pass the ZEREZ-ID to the grid operator (NELEV §4(9)), in practice through the installer. Can look up an ID without an account.
Enters the ZEREZ-IDs of the inverter, the storage system, the charger and the protection devices in the grid connection application.
Looks up the technical properties with the ID and continues without a PDF certificate. Refuses the final approval, or disconnects after notice, when a certificate is invalid.

Must submit every issued unit or component certificate to the register (NELEV §4(3)). A certification body issues the certificate. After a software update that changes certified properties, a new certificate and a new ID are needed. Since 2026 the manufacturer controls access to non-public parameters (secondary source).

FGW e.V. runs the register, assigns the ZEREZ-ID and the validity status, and provides accounts and interfaces. FGW states that it holds the register task under EnWG §49d(3); the official notice was not read. The Bundesnetzagentur has no ZEREZ role by law and plans to add location data by linking the MaStR to ZEREZ (a plan, not a duty).

explain.consequences: The final approval is refused when the duties are not met (NELEV §6(1)). A running plant with an invalid certificate can be disconnected after a written notice; the notice gives two months to fix it, one month for decoupling protection (§6(2)). explain.suggest: This is a suggestion, not a duty. For each product that needs a certificate, the passport can carry the ZEREZ-ID as the manufacturer gives it, the status and the date of the last check, as a link and not as a copy of the certificate. Until the manufacturer supplies an ID, the passport shows a specimen without a number. The passport never generates an ID. A firmware change can prompt a new check.
